title: Ezekiel 4:1–8
context: The LORD continues to address Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles by the river Chebar (1:1–3), calling him “son of man.” In 4:1–3 he tells the prophet to draw Jerusalem on a tile and act out a siege against it, with an iron pan set between him and the city as a wall. In 4:4–8 Ezekiel is to lie on his left side for the house of Israel and then on his right side for the house of Judah, bearing their iniquity: three hundred ninety days for Israel and forty days for Judah, each day standing for a year, as the text says. Readers reckon these numbers in different ways, some as a span of past sin and others as a period of punishment, with various starting points proposed; the notes endorse none and supply no dates. Both traditions read these sign-acts as acted prophecy, a visible sermon to people who would not listen to words alone.

verses.text: “You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel to take a tile and portray Jerusalem on it. Arminian readers note that God chooses a vivid, visible sign for exiles who had heard warnings before, giving them another opportunity to understand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD directing every detail of the prophet’s ministry, even the materials of his message. Both traditions read the tile as the start of an acted sermon, drawn on a common building material and set before the exiles’ eyes.

verses.text: Lay siege against it, build forts against it, and cast up a mound against it. Also set camps against it and plant battering rams against it all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel is to lay siege to the model city with forts, a mound, camps, and battering rams. Arminian readers see the sign anticipating Babylon’s siege, warning those who still hoped Jerusalem would stand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet plays the part of the besieger, picturing that the siege ultimately comes from the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the miniature siege as a clear, public message that Jerusalem’s fall was coming.

verses.text: Take for yourself an iron pan and set it for a wall of iron between you and the city. Then set your face toward it. It will be besieged, and you shall lay siege against it. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel sets an iron pan as a wall between himself and the city and sets his face against it, as a sign to Israel. Arminian readers often see the iron wall as a picture of separation that sin has created between the people and God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise suggest the iron pan may picture an unyielding barrier, or the firmness of the siege; the text calls it simply a sign. Both traditions read the gesture of setting the face as resolute judgment, and they hold the exact symbolism with care.

verses.text: “Moreover lie on your left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel on it. According to the number of the days that you shall lie on it, you shall bear their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel is to lie on his left side and lay Israel’s iniquity on it, bearing it for the number of days he lies there. Arminian readers see the prophet identifying with his people, embodying their guilt before their eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet bearing iniquity in a representative, symbolic way, not as an atonement. Shared ground: both traditions read the sign as acted judgment, and they note that bearing iniquity here means displaying its weight, not removing it.

verses.text: For I have appointed the years of their iniquity to be to you a number of days, even three hundred ninety days. So you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has appointed the years of Israel’s iniquity as days, three hundred ninety in all. Arminian readers note that the number is given plainly, while its reckoning has been worked out in more than one way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the figure as stated, a day for each year, and avoid fixing it to a single chronology. Both traditions read the long span as a measure of Israel’s persistent sin, and they leave the calculation open, endorsing no single scheme.

verses.text: “Again, when you have accomplished these, you shall lie on your right side, and shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah. I have appointed forty days, each day for a year, to you.
verses.arminianNotes: After those days, Ezekiel lies on his right side forty days for Judah, each day for a year. Arminian readers note the shorter figure for Judah and hear echoes of other forty-year spans, while holding any link loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the forty days as a defined period of judgment set by the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions present the numbers as the text gives them, recognize that readers compute them differently, and do not supply dates.

verses.text: You shall set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, with your arm uncovered; and you shall prophesy against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel sets his face toward the siege with his arm uncovered and prophesies against it. Arminian readers see the bared arm as readiness for action, a picture of the judgment that will soon fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the uncovered arm as an image of power, perhaps recalling the LORD’s own outstretched arm. Both traditions read the posture as determined, prophetic opposition to Jerusalem’s sin, while holding the image’s exact sense lightly.

verses.text: Behold, I put ropes on you, and you shall not turn yourself from one side to the other, until you have accomplished the days of your siege.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD puts ropes on Ezekiel so he cannot turn until the days of the siege are complete. Arminian readers note the prophet’s own submission, which these restraints make visible to onlookers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD binding his servant to the full length of the sign, so that nothing interrupts it. Shared ground: both traditions read the ropes as a sign that the siege cannot be escaped, without speculating on the physical details.
